questions.explanation: Audio files sit in object storage and reach listeners through a CDN, so a track starts from a server near them. The app talks to stateless API instances behind a gateway that checks the session with an auth service. Track and playlist metadata lives in a database with a cache in front, and catalog search uses a search index. Every play becomes an event on a queue; workers write the events to an archive for royalty reports and recommendations, so recording plays never slows playback down.

requirements.text: A track starts playing in under a second, anywhere in the world
Users browse and search a catalog of 100 million tracks
Every play is recorded for royalties and recommendations without slowing playback
Only signed-in users can stream
The service keeps working when one server fails

rules.text: Audio is streamed from a CDN backed by object storage
rules.explanation: Audio is most of the traffic. A CDN keeps popular tracks close to listeners and keeps the egress off your servers.

rules.text: API requests reach the services through a gateway or load balancer
rules.explanation: One entry point spreads traffic and routes around failed instances.

rules.text: At least two API instances
rules.explanation: One instance is a single point of failure.

rules.text: The gateway or API checks the session with an auth service
rules.explanation: Streaming is a paid product: every request must belong to a signed-in user.

rules.text: Track and playlist metadata lives in a database
rules.explanation: Albums, artists and playlists are structured and must survive restarts.

rules.text: Catalog search uses a search index
rules.explanation: Typo-tolerant, ranked search over 100 million titles needs an inverted index, not LIKE queries.

rules.text: Play events go to a queue, not straight to a database
rules.explanation: Billions of events a day would overload a database on the request path; a queue absorbs them.

rules.text: Workers move events from the queue into storage
rules.explanation: Royalty reports and recommendation jobs read the archived events later, in bulk.

rules.text: Popular metadata is cached
rules.explanation: The same albums and playlists are read millions of times a day.

rules.text: Clients never read storage or databases directly
rules.explanation: Audio goes through the CDN and data through the API, which checks access.

questions.explanation: Studios upload huge master files straight to object storage with a pre-signed URL. The upload API puts an encoding job on a queue, and a pool of encoders writes every resolution and bitrate back to storage, so players can switch quality as bandwidth changes. Viewers stream the segments from a CDN. The playback API records viewing positions in a wide-column store so any device can resume, and serves personalised rows from a cache that a scheduled batch job fills.

requirements.text: Studios upload master files of hundreds of gigabytes
Each title is encoded into many resolutions and bitrates
Playback starts quickly and adapts to the viewer's bandwidth
Viewers continue where they left off, on any device
The home page shows personalised rows that load instantly

rules.text: Masters upload straight to object storage
rules.explanation: Pushing hundreds of gigabytes through an API server wastes it; a pre-signed URL lets storage take the bytes.

rules.text: The upload service queues an encoding job
rules.explanation: Encoding takes hours; the request returns at once and the work happens in the background.

rules.text: Several encoders work in parallel
rules.explanation: One title becomes dozens of renditions; split the work.

rules.text: Encoders write the renditions back to object storage
rules.explanation: Each resolution and bitrate is stored as short segments the player can switch between.

rules.text: Viewers stream from a CDN in front of storage
rules.explanation: Video is most of the internet's traffic; Netflix puts caches inside internet providers.

rules.text: API calls go through a gateway or load balancer
rules.explanation: Spreads load and hides failed instances.

rules.text: Viewing positions are written to a wide-column store
rules.explanation: Millions of small writes a minute, read back by user and time: a good fit for Cassandra-style storage.

rules.text: Personalised rows are served from a cache
rules.explanation: Ranking at request time is too slow.

rules.text: A scheduled job precomputes recommendations
rules.explanation: Recommendations change slowly; compute them in batch and store the result.

questions.prompt: Design real-time collaborative editing like Google Docs
questions.explanation: Editors keep a WebSocket open to a gateway, which checks document permissions and forwards each edit to the collaboration service that owns the document. That service orders concurrent operations (operational transformation or CRDTs) and appends them to a per-document log, then broadcasts them back. Recently opened documents stay in a cache. A worker compacts the log into snapshots in object storage, which keeps old versions restorable and lets large documents open quickly.

requirements.text: Everyone editing a document sees the others' changes within a fraction of a second
Concurrent edits to the same paragraph never lose text
Old versions can be viewed and restored
Only people the document is shared with can open it
Opening a large document is fast

rules.text: Editors connect over WebSockets to a collaboration service
rules.explanation: Edits must be pushed both ways continuously; polling would be too slow and too costly.

rules.text: At least two WebSocket servers
rules.explanation: Millions of open connections don't fit on one server, and one server would be a single point of failure.

rules.text: Every operation is appended to a per-document log in a database
rules.explanation: One ordered log per document gives each edit a version, so concurrent edits can be transformed and none is lost.

rules.text: Permissions are checked before joining a document
rules.explanation: A shared link must not let anyone outside the sharing list read the document.

rules.text: Workers compact the log into snapshots in object storage
rules.explanation: Replaying years of operations is slow; periodic snapshots are the restore points for version history.

rules.text: Open documents are kept in a cache
rules.explanation: Active documents are read on every join and reload.

rules.text: Snapshot work is queued, not done on the edit path
rules.explanation: Compaction is heavy; a queue keeps it from slowing typing down.

rules.text: Clients never talk to the database or storage
rules.explanation: All edits must be ordered and permission-checked by the service.

questions.prompt: Design group chat like Discord or Slack
questions.explanation: Clients keep a WebSocket to one of many gateway servers. A message goes to the messages service, which stores it in a wide-column database partitioned by channel and time, then publishes it on a pub/sub bus; every gateway with members of that channel pushes it to them. An indexer worker reads the same stream into a search index. A rate limiter in front stops spam floods.

requirements.text: A message reaches everyone online in the channel within a second
Servers with 100,000 members and millions of concurrent connections
History is kept forever and loads newest first
Users can search old messages

rules.text: Clients connect through WebSocket gateways
rules.explanation: Messages are pushed, not polled.

rules.text: Several gateway servers
rules.explanation: Millions of connections are spread across many gateways.

rules.text: Messages fan out to gateways through pub/sub
rules.explanation: The sender's gateway doesn't know where the other members are connected; a bus delivers to all of them.

rules.text: Messages are stored in a wide-column store
rules.explanation: Partitioning by channel and time bucket makes 'latest 50 messages' one fast read, even at trillions of rows.

rules.text: An indexer feeds a search index from the message stream
rules.explanation: Searching trillions of messages needs an inverted index, updated asynchronously.

rules.text: A rate limiter stops spam floods
rules.explanation: One bot must not be able to flood a channel.

rules.text: Clients never talk to the stores directly
rules.explanation: Permissions and ordering are enforced by the service.

questions.explanation: Clients split files into blocks named by their hash. They ask the metadata API which blocks are new (a block index in a key-value store makes duplicates free) and upload only those straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs, so an interrupted upload resumes from the last block. File and folder metadata lives in a relational database with transactions. Each change is published on a queue, and a notification service pushes it over a long-lived connection to the user's other devices.

requirements.text: Files of many gigabytes upload, and an interrupted upload resumes
A change on one device appears on the user's other devices within seconds
Identical content is stored only once
Folder listings and file versions are always consistent
The service keeps working when one server fails

rules.text: Clients upload blocks straight to object storage
rules.explanation: Big uploads shouldn't pass through API servers; per-block uploads also make resuming trivial.

rules.text: Metadata lives in a relational database
rules.explanation: Moves and renames must be atomic.

rules.text: Block hashes are indexed in a key-value store
rules.explanation: Looking up a block by its hash lets the client skip anything already stored.

rules.text: Devices hold a connection to a notification service
rules.explanation: Devices learn about changes at once.

rules.text: Changes are published through a queue to the notifier
rules.explanation: The API that saved the change doesn't know where the user's other devices are connected.

rules.text: API requests go through a load balancer
rules.explanation: Routes around failed instances.

rules.text: At least two API instances
rules.explanation: One instance is a single point of failure.

rules.text: Clients never touch the databases
rules.explanation: Only the API may change metadata.

questions.prompt: Design ticket sales for a sold-out concert like Ticketmaster
questions.explanation: A virtual waiting room in front admits fans at the rate the booking service can handle. Seats and orders live in a relational database, where a conditional update or row lock makes double selling impossible. A chosen seat is held in Redis with a 10-minute expiry while the fan pays. Payment confirmation goes through a queue to workers that use idempotency keys, so a double click never charges twice; a scheduler releases holds that expired without payment.

requirements.text: 2 million fans arrive in the first minute for 50,000 seats
A seat is never sold twice
A chosen seat is held for 10 minutes while the fan pays
A retry or double click never charges twice

rules.text: A waiting room admits fans at a safe rate
rules.explanation: Letting everyone in at once overloads the database; a waiting room is fairer than random errors.

rules.text: At least two booking instances
rules.explanation: Peak traffic needs horizontal capacity.

rules.text: Seats and orders are in a relational database
rules.explanation: A transaction with a row lock or a conditional UPDATE guarantees one buyer per seat.

rules.text: Seat holds live in a cache with a TTL
rules.explanation: An expiring key releases the seat automatically if the fan walks away.

rules.text: Payments run through a queue and workers
rules.explanation: Payment providers are slow and flaky; a queue retries safely, and idempotency keys stop double charges.

rules.text: A scheduler releases expired holds
rules.explanation: Seats from abandoned checkouts go back on sale.

rules.text: Event pages come from a CDN
rules.explanation: Static pages shouldn't touch the booking servers.

rules.text: Clients never reach the stores directly
rules.explanation: All bookings go through the service.

questions.prompt: Design a payments API like Stripe
questions.explanation: Merchants call the API through a rate limiter and a gateway that validates their API key. The payments service stores an idempotency key with each request in the same transaction as the charge, so a retry returns the first result. Money movements are rows in an append-only double-entry ledger, replicated to a standby. Events are written to an outbox and published on a queue; webhook workers deliver them, and a scheduler retries failed deliveries with backoff.

requirements.text: A retried request never creates a second charge
Every money movement is recorded and survives a database failure
Merchants are notified of events, with retries if their server is down
Only merchants with a valid API key can create charges
One merchant's burst can't take the API down for others

rules.text: Requests pass through an API gateway
rules.explanation: One place to authenticate and route.

rules.text: The gateway validates API keys with an auth service
rules.explanation: No key, no charge.

rules.text: A rate limiter in front of the API
rules.explanation: Per-merchant limits isolate noisy neighbours.

rules.text: Charges and idempotency keys are in a relational database
rules.explanation: A unique key stored in the same transaction as the charge makes retries safe.

rules.text: The ledger database replicates to a standby
rules.explanation: Losing committed payments is not acceptable; a synchronous standby takes over.

rules.text: Events go through a queue to webhook workers
rules.explanation: Written to an outbox in the payment's transaction, then published, so no event is lost or invented.

rules.text: A scheduler retries failed webhooks
rules.explanation: Merchant servers go down; retries with exponential backoff over days.

rules.text: Merchants never reach the database
rules.explanation: All writes are validated by the service.

questions.prompt: Design a web crawler and search engine like Google
questions.explanation: A scheduler decides which URLs are due and feeds a URL frontier queue. Many crawler workers take URLs from it, check per-host timing and cached robots.txt in a shared cache to stay polite, store the raw pages in object storage and push newly found links back onto the frontier. Indexer workers build an inverted index from the pages. A query service behind a load balancer answers searches from the index and caches popular queries.

requirements.text: Crawl billions of pages and recrawl popular ones often
Never hit one site too fast, and respect robots.txt
Keep the raw pages so the index can be rebuilt
Answer searches in under 200 ms

rules.text: A scheduler feeds a URL frontier queue that crawlers consume
rules.explanation: The frontier decides what to fetch next and how often to come back.

rules.text: Many crawler workers
rules.explanation: Billions of pages need thousands of parallel fetches.

rules.text: Crawlers share per-host timing and robots.txt in a cache
rules.explanation: Every crawler must know when a host was last hit and what it allows.

rules.text: Raw pages are stored in object storage
rules.explanation: Re-indexing must not mean re-crawling.

rules.text: Indexers build a search index
rules.explanation: An inverted index maps words to pages.

rules.text: Searches go through a load balancer to a query service
rules.explanation: Spreads the load.

rules.text: The query service reads the index
rules.explanation: Answers come from the index, never from crawling.

rules.text: Popular queries are cached
rules.explanation: A small share of queries is most of the traffic.

rules.text: Users never query the index directly
rules.explanation: The service ranks and filters results.

questions.prompt: Design live streaming with chat like Twitch
questions.explanation: The streamer sends one high-quality stream to an ingest service near them. Transcoder workers turn it into several qualities and write short segments and playlists to storage, and viewers fetch them through a CDN, so a million viewers cost the origin almost nothing and stay a few seconds behind. Chat is separate: viewers hold WebSockets to chat gateways, and a pub/sub bus fans each message out to every gateway.

requirements.text: Streamers send one high-quality stream
Viewers can choose from several qualities
Viewers are only a few seconds behind the streamer
A single stream can have a million viewers
Viewers chat live with each other

rules.text: Streams reach an ingest service through a load balancer
rules.explanation: Ingest servers are spread out so streamers connect to one close by.

rules.text: Ingest hands the stream to transcoders
rules.explanation: Each quality is a separate encode.

rules.text: Transcoders write short segments to storage
rules.explanation: Two-second segments and a playlist keep viewers close to live.

rules.text: Viewers watch through a CDN
rules.explanation: A million viewers must not hit the origin.

rules.text: Chat runs over WebSockets
rules.explanation: Messages are pushed instantly.

rules.text: Chat messages fan out through pub/sub
rules.explanation: Viewers of one channel are spread over many gateways.

rules.text: Viewers never read the origin storage directly
rules.explanation: That would bypass the CDN.

questions.prompt: Design a distributed job scheduler like Airflow
questions.explanation: Users define jobs through an API that stores definitions and runs in a relational database. Two or more schedulers claim due runs from that database with row locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED), so a run is started once even if a scheduler crashes. Claimed runs go on a queue to a pool of workers, which record each attempt in the database and ship logs to object storage. Runs that keep failing move to a dead-letter queue.

requirements.text: Millions of jobs start at their scheduled time, to the minute
A run starts once, even if a scheduler crashes or two run at the same time
Failed runs retry and end in a dead-letter queue after too many attempts
Users see each run's status and logs

rules.text: Users manage jobs through an API behind a load balancer
rules.explanation: One entry point.

rules.text: Jobs and runs live in a relational database
rules.explanation: Runs and their state need transactions.

rules.text: At least two schedulers
rules.explanation: One scheduler is a single point of failure.

rules.text: Schedulers claim due runs from the database
rules.explanation: Row locks with SKIP LOCKED let several schedulers share the work without starting a run twice.

rules.text: Runs go through a queue to workers
rules.explanation: Workers scale separately from schedulers.

rules.text: A pool of workers
rules.explanation: Jobs run in parallel.

rules.text: Workers record each attempt
rules.explanation: Retries need to know how many attempts were made.

rules.text: A separate dead-letter queue
rules.explanation: Poison jobs must stop retrying and wait for a person.

rules.text: Workers ship logs to object storage
rules.explanation: Logs are large and read rarely.
